title: Futures Tick Value: Complete Guide to Calculation, Contract Specs, and Risk Management
summary: Futures tick value is the dollar amount of a contract's minimum price move, calculated as tick size multiplied by the point value (contract multiplier). This guide covers tick value definitions, reference tables for equity index, energy, metals, currency, and crypto futures, step-by-step P&L formulas, risk management techniques, and how to trade futures on Webull.
body_markdown:
Every futures trade ultimately comes down to the **futures tick value** . Whether you are sizing a position, setting a stop, or calculating profit and loss on E-mini S&P 500 tick value or crude oil contracts, the tick value converts price movement into real dollars. This guide covers the core definitions, contract-by-contract reference tables, step-by-step P&L formulas, and how to apply tick value when trading futures on Webull.


---


## Key Takeaways


-


**Futures tick value** is the dollar amount of the minimum price move in a given contract.


-


Tick Value = Tick Size x Point Value (the contract multiplier).


-


The same tick count represents very different dollar amounts across different contracts; always size positions in dollars, not ticks.


-


Micro futures contracts are one-tenth the size of standard contracts, offering more granular risk control.


-


Webull offers futures trading across indices, energies, metals, currencies, agriculture, interest rates, and cryptocurrencies for eligible US residents.

## Part 1. What Is Futures Tick Value and How Is It Defined?


Futures contracts trade through regulated exchanges such as the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) or the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX). Each contract has standardized specifications, including the minimum price increment allowed. Understanding these specs is a prerequisite for trading.


### 1.1 Tick Size, Tick Value, and Point Value: Key Definitions


Three distinct but linked terms govern every futures P&L calculation. Mixing them up is one of the most common and costly errors a futures trader can make.


**Tick size** is the smallest increment by which a futures contract's price can move. It is set by the exchange and varies by product. For the E-mini S&P 500 (ES), the tick size is 0.25 index points. For WTI Crude Oil (CL), it is $0.01 per barrel.


**Tick value** is the dollar amount that one tick move represents. For ES, one tick is worth $12.50. This amount is credited to or debited from your account each time price moves by the minimum increment.


**Point value** (also called the contract multiplier) is the dollar value of a full one-point move. For ES, one full index point is worth $50. This is the foundational multiplier from which tick value is derived.


The three values are connected by a single formula:


**Tick Value = Tick Size x Point Value**


For ES: 0.25 x $50 = $12.50. If you know any two values, you can always calculate the third. The contract multiplier can also be derived by dividing tick value by tick size (Tick Value / Tick Size = Point Value).


A common error is stating "ES is $12.50 per point." That understates each point move by a factor of four. ES is $12.50 per tick and $50 per point.

## Part 3. How to Calculate Futures P&L Using Tick Value


Once you know a contract's tick value, calculating profit or loss is straightforward. Two equivalent methods exist: working in ticks or working in points. Both produce the same result, since tick value already incorporates the point value multiplier.


### 3.1 The Core P&L Formulas


**Method 1: Working in ticks (preferred for scalpers)**


P&L = Ticks Moved x Tick Value x Number of Contracts


**Method 2: Working in points (preferred for swing traders)**


P&L = Points Moved x Point Value x Number of Contracts


Both formulas are mathematically equivalent. Working in ticks is natural for traders who track minimum price increments. Working in points suits traders who think in index levels or price handles.


### 3.2 Worked Examples Across Key Contracts


**Example 1: E-mini S&P 500 (ES) — Long trade**


A trader buys 2 ES contracts at 5,000.00 and exits at 5,012.50.


-


Points moved: 5,012.50 - 5,000.00 = 12.50 points


-


Ticks moved: 12.50 / 0.25 = 50 ticks


-


Gross P&L: 50 ticks x $12.50 x 2 contracts = $1,250


-


Less commissions (example: $4 per contract round-turn x 2 = $8): Net P&L = $1,242


The same price move in the opposite direction on a short position would result in a loss of $1,250 gross before fees.


**Example 2: WTI Crude Oil (CL) — Computing ticks from a price move**


A trader buys 1 CL contract at $53.60, and price moves to $54.00.


-


Price move: $0.40


-


Ticks moved: $0.40 / $0.01 = 40 ticks


-


Gross P&L: 40 ticks x $10.00 x 1 contract = $400


The 1,000-barrel contract size means even a $0.01 tick is worth $10. Contract size has a significant multiplying effect on P&L.


**Example 3: Reverse calculation from dollar P&L to points**


A trader realizes a $450 gross gain on an NQ trade.


-


Points from P&L: $450 / $20 = 22.5 points moved


This reverse calculation is useful for reconstructing a trade's price move from a known P&L figure.

## Part 4. Why Futures Tick Value Is Central to Risk Management


Futures trading uses leverage. You control a large notional position with a relatively small margin deposit. This means tick value directly determines how quickly a position can gain or lose value. Ignoring tick value when sizing positions is a primary cause of oversized losses in futures trading.


### 4.1 Stop Placement and Position Sizing with Tick Value


**Calculating dollar risk before entering a trade:**


Dollar Risk = Stop Distance (in ticks) x Tick Value x Number of Contracts


Example: Long NQ, 20-tick stop, 2 contracts:
Dollar Risk = 20 x $5.00 x 2 = **$200**


**Calculating contracts to match a target dollar risk:**


Contracts = Risk Budget / (Stop Distance x Tick Value)


Example: Risk budget $500 on CL, 30-tick stop:
Contracts = $500 / (30 x $10.00) = 1.67, rounded down to **1 contract**


These formulas let traders define risk in dollar terms first, then determine contract quantity. This approach is more rigorous than sizing from margin alone, because tick value is fixed by the exchange while margin requirements can vary by broker and change with volatility.


Tick values also affect bid/ask spread impact and stop order placement. Setting stop orders without accounting for tick increments can result in rejected orders or unintended risk exposure.


### 4.2 Common Tick Value Mistakes to Avoid


Understanding these frequent errors can help traders approach futures more carefully:


-


**Confusing tick value with point value.** Saying "ES is $12.50 per point" understates each full point move by a factor of four. ES is $12.50 per tick and $50 per point.


-


**Sizing by tick count rather than dollar value.** A 20-tick stop is $250 on ES but only $25 on MES. Never equate tick counts across contracts.


-


**Forgetting the contract count.** P&L scales linearly with the number of contracts held. Always multiply through.


-


**Omitting commissions and exchange fees.** On short-duration trades of a few ticks, round-turn costs can be material relative to gross P&L.


-


**Assuming all index futures share the same multiplier.** ES is $50 per point, NQ is $20 per point, and YM is $5 per point. The formulas are the same, but the constants differ by contract.

## Part 5. Trading Futures on Webull: Account Setup, Margin, and Supported Contracts


[Webull](https://www.webull.com/) offers futures trading to eligible US residents through a dedicated futures account. The platform provides access to contracts across seven categories, alongside the order types and account tools needed to put tick value knowledge into practice.


### 5.1 Eligibility and Account Opening


To open a Webull futures account, the following conditions must be met:


-


You must be a US resident.


-


You must hold an existing individual Webull brokerage account (joint accounts cannot serve as the basis for a futures account application).


-


You must be approved for futures trading within the Webull platform.


**To open a futures account via the Webull mobile app:**


1.


Tap the Menu icon.


2.


Select Settings.


3.


Tap Account Management.


4.


Scroll down and select Apply for new accounts.


5.


Choose Futures and follow the application prompts.


**To open a futures account via the Webull desktop app:**


1.


Click the drop-down in the top-right corner where your account number appears.


2.


Select Futures.


3.


On the My Account page, scroll down and select Futures.


4.


Follow the prompts to complete the application.


To place any trade, you must meet the applicable margin requirement for the specific contract you intend to trade. Visit the[Webull futures page](https://www.webull.com/trading-investing/futures) to explore available contracts and begin your application.


### 5.2 Funding Methods and Margin Requirements


Webull futures accounts can be funded through three methods:


-


**Internal transfer:** Move cash from your linked Webull brokerage account through the Transfer Money section in the app or on the website. This is the fastest funding method.


-


**ACH deposit:** Deposit directly into the futures account via ACH. ACH deposits typically settle within 2 to 3 business days and do not provide Instant Buying Power.


-


**Wire transfer:** Submit a wire through the Transfer Money section. Wire instructions are provided after selecting the futures account as the destination. Include your Webull Futures account number in the memo field when wiring funds.


Webull futures accounts use three margin tiers:


**Intraday margin** is the lowest margin requirement, available for eligible contracts generally between 9:00 AM and 4:15 PM ET, for positions not intended to be held through the close. Intraday margin increases leverage, which can amplify losses as well as potential gains, and may not be suitable for all traders.


**Initial margin** is the equity required when opening a position intended to be held through the end of intraday hours, or when entering outside intraday hours. It is typically between 3% and 12% of the contract's notional value, depending on the contract and market conditions. Because futures are leveraged instruments, this margin deposit represents only a fraction of the full contract value.


**Maintenance margin** is the minimum equity required to hold a position beyond intraday hours after the initial margin has been posted. It is lower than initial margin and varies by position. If your account falls below the maintenance margin level, Webull will require you to deposit additional funds to restore the account to the initial margin level. If you do not, Webull may liquidate your position.


For a full list of margin requirements across all supported futures products, visit the[Webull Futures Margin Rates page](https://www.webull.com/trading-investing/futures) . Rates vary by service provider; please refer to the latest pricing.


### 5.3 Supported Contracts, Order Types, and Trading Hours


Webull provides access to futures contracts across seven categories: indices, interest rates, currencies, agriculture, metals, energies, and cryptocurrencies. Futures are traded through exchanges such as the CME or NYMEX; customers place orders through Webull.


**Available order types for futures on Webull:**


-


Market orders


-


Limit orders


-

-


Stop market orders


-

-


OCO (One-Cancels-the-Other) orders


With OCO orders, both parts of the order are live in the market simultaneously. Due to market volatility, it is possible for both legs to execute. Cancellations are on a best-efforts basis, and use of OCO orders involves acceptance of the associated risks.
